summary: Describes how the IETF's separate standards fit together to support emergency calls over the Internet, from citizens and visitors to the authorities. It is informational and ties together location, call routing and signaling pieces. It was later updated by RFC 7852.

eli5.summary: Calling for help on the internet needs several pieces to work together. This document is the map showing how all those pieces fit so your call reaches the right emergency helpers.

questions: how do internet emergency calls work
what is the sos service urn
how does lost route emergency calls
subtitle: The map showing how location, call routing and SIP signaling fit together so an Internet emergency call reaches the right call center.

tldr.problem: Calling for help over the Internet needs many separate IETF pieces, run by different parties, to cooperate: the device, the access network, the service provider and the emergency call center.
tldr.mechanism: The framework marks the call with an emergency service URN, has the endpoint learn its location from the access network, maps that location to a call center with LoST, and carries the location in the SIP INVITE.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational framework, not a standard, and it defers normative behavior to a separate best-current-practice document. It was later updated by RFC 7852.

facts.label: NENA call setup target
facts.value: 2 seconds from last dial press to ring at the PSAP

today: RFC 6443 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 7852. It was not obsoleted, and it states that normative requirements for devices and networks live in a separate best-current-practice document.

sections.title: Scope and Goals
sections.content:
RFC 6443 describes how a person places a call to a Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP), a call center set up by response agencies to accept emergency calls. These citizen-or-visitor-to-authority calls are different from authority-to-authority calls and from warning systems that go from authorities to citizens.

The document focuses on Internet devices placing emergency calls and on PSAPs that handle Internet multimedia calls natively. It uses the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and supports sessions of any media type, negotiated with the existing SIP offer/answer mechanisms. Gateways to legacy telephone systems, which route on telephone numbers, are left to national standards and are out of scope.

Because it is a framework, it contains no normative behavior. Emergency calling needs no new SIP header fields, methods, status codes or message bodies; it needs existing mechanisms used in specific ways. From the PSAP's view, three things matter: the call goes to the most appropriate PSAP based on the caller's location, the PSAP can automatically obtain a location accurate enough to dispatch help, and the PSAP can re-establish a session to the caller if the original is disrupted.
sections.eli5: When you dial for help, three things must happen: your call must go to the right helpers, they must find out where you are, and they must be able to call you back if the line drops.

sections.title: How an Emergency Call Is Placed
sections.content:
An emergency call is recognized by a unique service URN, urn:service:sos when one number covers all emergencies (RFC 5031). Users are not expected to dial a URN. The device detects a local or home emergency dial string and translates it into the URN, which goes in the Request-URI of the INVITE. The RFC prefers that the endpoint does this translation, because emergency calls carry location in the signaling and ordinary calls normally do not. A proxy can step in if the endpoint fails to recognize the dial string.

The typical flow for an Ethernet phone has these steps. The phone connects to its access network and learns its location, then registers with a SIP registrar and makes an initial LoST query that returns the local emergency dial string and a PSAP URI. When the user dials, the phone refreshes its location and the LoST mapping, falling back on cached values if either is slow or fails. It then sends an INVITE carrying the service URN, the PSAP URI and the location in a Geolocation header (RFC 6442).

The INVITE passes through the outgoing proxy to an Emergency Services Routing Proxy (ESRP), the incoming proxy of the emergency services domain, which picks the actual PSAP. A proxy in the PSAP selects an available call taker. The 200 OK travels back along the same path and the ACK completes setup, and the call taker sees the caller's location.

Emergency practitioners consider a single-button emergency call interface undesirable because it causes a very high rate of false or accidental calls. They recommend that devices start emergency calls only from entry of specific emergency dial strings and that speed dial not be permitted for this.
sections.eli5: Your phone works out where it is, asks a lookup service which emergency center covers that spot, and sends the call there with your location attached, like writing your address on the envelope.

sections.title: Location and How It Is Obtained
sections.content:
Location is central because it serves two purposes: routing the call and dispatching responders. The RFC separates the routing location, which may be coarse, from the dispatch location, which has to be precise enough to find the caller. Mobile systems often route on a coarse location such as the serving cell site and sector, then update it once a better fix is known. The text says a cold start of some measurement mechanisms can take as much as 30 seconds, too long to wait for an emergency.

Location comes in civic form (a street address, possibly with floor and room), geospatial form (longitude, latitude and altitude on a datum such as WGS84) and cell tower/sector form. The RFC advises sending location in the form in which it was determined, because converting between civic and geo needs a database, and converting with a different database than the PSAP uses risks errors. An error of a single house number can send responders to the wrong building.

An endpoint can obtain location from the access network using a Location Configuration Protocol: DHCP (civic or geo), HELD over HTTP, or LLDP-MED. No single protocol can be mandated for every network, so a separate best-current-practice document sets a list of protocols that every emergency-capable endpoint must implement and that every access network must provide at least one of. The endpoint conveys the result to the PSAP as a PIDF-LO object in SIP.

Other points the RFC makes: location may be sent by value or by reference; if several locations exist, the element that chooses the route must pick exactly one to use with LoST, and an original (measured) location must be preferred over a derived one; location should be validated before use, but a location that fails validation is still better than no location; and if the network cannot determine location it must supply a default location marked as such.
sections.eli5: Helpers need to know where you are. The phone can be told its address by the network, can measure it itself, or can be set by a person. The address has to be sent as it was found, because translating it can make mistakes.

sections.title: Routing the Call to the PSAP
sections.content:
Routing uses one or more criteria in the INVITE: the caller's location, the type of emergency service (for example fire, police or ambulance, marked with the service identifier) and the media capabilities of the caller, since some call centers handle text or video separately from voice. Location of the caller is always the primary input, even when the call is made on someone else's behalf.

The mapping is done by the Location-to-Service Translation protocol (LoST, RFC 5222). A LoST query carries a location, civic or geo, plus a service identifier, and returns one or more URIs. Normal SIP routing resolves the URI to a next hop. The LoST server should return a simple polygon with few points so a small mobile device can tell cheaply when it has left the covered area. The server is normally run by the local emergency authorities.

Endpoints discover a LIS and a LoST server through DHCP options. For LoST the recommended priority is DHCP first, a provisioned value second, and a DNS SRV query in the SIP domain third. If the endpoint cannot do the mapping, the outbound proxy may do it, but a proxy cannot ask an endpoint for its location, because that would let any proxy on the path make the endpoint reveal it. The ESRP can use PSAP state, caller location and other criteria to route onward, and to route on media it needs an SDP offer in the initial INVITE.
sections.eli5: A lookup service works like a phone book of helpers: you tell it where you are and what kind of help you need, and it tells you which call center to ring.

sections.title: Signaling, Call Backs and Media
sections.content:
A user agent that does its own recognition and routing builds an INVITE with the service URN in the Request-URI, the LoST-determined PSAP URI in a Route header and the location in a Geolocation header. It must include callback identifiers in the Contact and From headers and should include an SDP offer. At least one proxy on the path must be able to help user agents that cannot do these steps: it can tell that location is missing from the absence of a Geolocation header, and that dial-string recognition was missing when the local dial string appears in the From header without the service URN.

The call taker must be able to reach the caller again. The Contact header must carry a globally routable URI, and an address of record must also be given, either in the From header with SIP Identity or as a network-asserted URI. A PSAP ends a call with a normal BYE, and the RFC calls it undesirable for the caller to terminate. Call waiting, transfer, three-way calling and hold should be disabled during an emergency call, and call forwarding should be disabled because it can interfere with PSAP callbacks.

PSAPs should always accept RTP media, real-time text and G.711 A-law voice (and mu-law in North America). They should accept instant messaging with at least the pager-mode MESSAGE request and MSRP. Video is needed to support Video Relay Service as well as modern video phones. Secure RTP with DTLS keying is desirable.

The RFC also asks for an automated test procedure, described in the separate best-current-practice document, that checks routing, signaling and the media path without using PSAP staff. Devices should randomize when they run the boot-time test, to avoid an avalanche of tests after a large power outage, and the PSAP may suspend the test if it is abused.
sections.eli5: The call carries your callback address so the helper can ring you again, and it turns off things like call waiting so nothing gets in the way. Devices also practice the call quietly now and then to make sure it still works.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to RFC 5069 and RFC 6280 for the security considerations of emergency calling. It suggests protecting location, identity and other private call data hop by hop with TLS or IPsec. S/MIME encryption of SIP signaling is not usable because it would hide location from the proxies that route on it.

The notable trade-off is stated plainly: if the attempt to set up a security association fails, the call should be retried without security. It is more important to get an emergency call through than to protect the data, and in many jurisdictions privacy is explicitly waived for emergency calls. The alternative of failing the call is considered unacceptable, even though a call without security may reveal user information including location.
sections.eli5: The call is locked in an envelope when it can be. If the lock does not work, it is sent anyway, because getting help matters more than keeping the address private.

items.title: User-entered
items.text: Kept by the user or installer; almost always less reliable than measured or wire database data.

items.title: Wire database
items.text: The access network maps a switch port or wire pair to a location.

items.title: End system measured
items.text: A GNSS receiver in the device; can take tens of seconds to start.

items.title: Network measured
items.text: The access network triangulates the device, for example with TDOA or AOA.
